claims.text: The applicable alloy is equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
Rapid quenching produces a chemically disordered, single-phase solid solution in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
The rapidly quenched CoCrFeNiTi state has favorable plasticity and machinability.
The pristine CoCrFeNiTi state has low hardness and strength.
Easy dislocation glide and rapid dynamic recovery govern the low hardness and strength of pristine CoCrFeNiTi.
Mild thermal annealing can induce short-range chemical ordering in the single-phase CoCrFeNiTi solid solution.
Annealing can induce short-range ordering without triggering a phase transformation.
Short-range chemical order acts as an intrinsic barrier to dislocation motion.
Annealing-induced atomic-scale ordering increases lattice friction.
The increased lattice friction impedes dislocation glide.
Reduced dislocation mobility suppresses dynamic recovery.
Suppression of dynamic recovery enhances work hardening.
Annealed samples will have higher yield strength than pristine rapidly quenched samples.
Annealed samples will have higher hardness than pristine rapidly quenched samples.
In situ deformation observations of annealed samples will reveal increased dislocation pinning and altered dislocation-density evolution.
The proposed comparison applies only while both states remain single-phase solid solutions and loading does not induce additional phase transformations.
The controlled comparison should use identical room-temperature conditions and strain rates for the quenched and annealed samples.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis identifies the absence of ordering, easy glide, and rapid recovery as causes of low hardness and strength, whereas the falsification rule describes short-range ordering itself as responsible for the low hardness and strength of the pristine alloy.
